newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: FORECAST-Irish 1996 EBR seen at 250-400 mln punts.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-Irish 1996 EBR seen at 250-400 mln punts.

text.p: Ireland's 1996 Exchequer Borrowing Requirement (EBR) is expected to be well below target at 250 to 400 million punts, helped by strong growth in tax revenues, economists said on Thursday.

They said the annual EBR figure, due to be released at 1630 GMT on Friday, would considerably undershoot the government's target of 729 million punts, although the exact figure would depend on how the government juggled its finances between 1996 and 1997.
Economists said tax revenues would be up by around 11 percent year-on-year, but other components of the EBR were less easy to predict.
"The big question is what the capital deficit will be," said Padhraic Garvey, senior economist at Riada Stockbrokers. Riada is forecasting an EBR of 350 million punts.
"We're looking for a current account surplus of about 300 million and capital deficit of around 650 million," Garvey said. "But the capital deficit could be lower."
NCB Stockbrokers forecast an EBR of 345 million, while Goodbody Stockbrokers was at the bottom end of expectations with a forecast of 250 million.
"We are certainly very bullish on the public finances," said Goodbody's Aisling Reilly. "But the actual figure all depends on how they decide to juggle the figures."
Alan McQuaid, chief eceonomist at Bloxham Stockbrokers, forecast an EBR of 400 million punts but said the figure could be as low as 250 million.
"Revenue will be up around 11 percent, which will imply a strong carry-over into this year," he said.
"It's an extremely comfortable situation. People know that they're going to juggle the figures around but everybody knows its going to be a good number."
Analysts said the figure was unlikely to have a major impact on Irish markets unless it sprang a major surprise.
"The story of the good public finances is already priced in, so probably it's not going to have much of an impact," Goodbody's Reilly said.
Garvey at Riada said a figure of around 350 million would not have a great effect on the bonds market.

"People will be interested in the breakdown between capital and current items. They will also be interested to see if they say whether they will carry forward into next year the savings they made below the target," he said.
"Apart from that, I don't think the market is expecting any great surprises".
